query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The naturally formed thin iron oxide film on as-received Q235 steel acts as a protective diffusion barrier during high‐temperature salt exposure, reducing degradation. Disrupting this oxide layer will lead to accelerated corrosion, while pre‐oxidizing to enhance the oxide layer’s integrity will offer improved corrosion resistance relative to untreated Q235 steel.
generation.material_initial_state: Commercial as-received Q235 steel exhibiting its naturally formed, thin, continuous iron oxide (Fe2O3/Fe3O4) film.
generation.intervention: Twofold: (1) Mechanically or thermally disrupt the native oxide layer on one set of samples, and (2) pre-oxidize another set to grow a thicker or more adherent oxide film. Use untreated as-received samples as a baseline.
generation.conditions: Experiments should be conducted under both room-temperature corrosive exposures and aggressive high-temperature conditions (e.g., molten salt exposure at approximately 700 °C). The protective effect of the oxide film is hypothesized to be significant only when the film is intact; its role is less critical under room-temperature conditions where the reaction kinetics are slower.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity, adherence, and microstructural quality of the iron oxide scale (a mixture of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4) that develops on Q235 steel.
generation.mechanism: An intact oxide film limits the inward diffusion of corrosive species (e.g., molten salt constituents) and the outward diffusion of iron ions, thereby slowing down corrosion processes. If the film is absent or disrupted, the underlying metal is exposed, leading to accelerated mass loss and degradation. Enhanced oxide formation through controlled pre-oxidation should strengthen this barrier effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature (700 °C) salt exposure, samples with an intact or enhanced (pre-oxidized) oxide film will show lower mass loss, reduced pit density, and less surface degradation than samples with a deliberately disrupted oxide film. At room temperature, differences between the groups will be minimal due to lower kinetic rates.
generation.baseline: As-received Q235 steel with its natural oxide film, subjected to both room-temperature and high-temperature exposures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily when the corrosion mechanism is governed by the integrity of the surface oxide layer. It may not hold in conditions where alternative corrosion mechanisms (such as localized pitting due to aggressive ionic species independent of the oxide film) dominate the degradation process.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how variations in minor alloying elements in Q235 steel (or environmental contaminants) might interact with the oxide film to influence corrosion kinetics under different thermal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three groups of Q235 steel samples: one with the natural as-received oxide layer, one where the oxide layer has been mechanically/thermally removed, and one pre-oxidized to enhance the oxide layer. Expose all groups to molten salt at 700 °C for a fixed duration and also to a room-temperature corrosive environment to serve as control. Compare the resulting weight changes, corrosion pit densities, and oxide phase integrity via SEM and XRD.
measurements: Surface morphology and oxide layer integrity (using SEM)
Phase analysis of the surface oxides (using XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under high-temperature molten salt exposure, samples with a disrupted oxide layer do not show significantly higher mass loss and corrosion damage compared to both the as-received and pre-oxidized samples, then the hypothesis that the oxide layer mediates corrosion protection is falsified.

Corrosion and Thermal Stability of CrMnFeNi High Entropy Alloy in Molten FLiBe Salt

Abstract: AbstractThe corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5, which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions.Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys

Conclusions: The corrosion resistance of Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy in molten salts was tested after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours. The alloy lost significant mass compared to reference 316 H stainless steel which was attributed to the dissolution of Mn into the salt.
